job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Ivan Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Ivan, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat above a fish and chip shop in Harbourtown with two guys from my course, and the smell gets into everything. Days are a bit of a patchwork. Mornings I send cold emails to start-ups and agencies, usually with an AI helper to draft and a human edit to make it sound like me. Afternoons I make short videos and posts for a local gym, Ironside Fitness, for a small fee. Evenings I learn a bit of data analysis online and go out for a run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the degree go, and how did the gym gig start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a marketing degree at Harbour University and passed with an average mark, no internship, because I was working in a call centre in the evenings. My final project was a campaign plan for a surf shop that nobody ever used, which stung a bit. The gym gig started because I went in for a workout and offered to fix their Instagram. They pay me a hundred and ten pounds a month, which is more of a tip than a wage. I owe a big student loan, I've got about ten days of savings, and my parents can't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about right, it's a nice tool and a lot of noise. I'd tell my flatmates that I already save an hour a day with it, so I'm not going to pretend it's nothing. Online I'd post what I've learned, but I wouldn't claim it's magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means the job market stays as tough as it is, but I stay a step ahead of the average applicant. There are too few marketing jobs in Harbourtown, and the ones that exist ask for a portfolio I'm still building. So it's the slow grind, but a grind I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the gym gig into more local clients, a cafe, a physio and a salon, aiming for six paying clients by spring. I'd apply for a dozen jobs a week and send a short video pitch with each, not a CV. And I'd finish my data course so I can show reporting, not only posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. A bit impatient, and a bit broke, but not scared. I feel like I'm building something, even if it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that make this picture easier for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit, because I'm already used to working with it. But it doesn't create jobs on its own. Everyone my age will soon use it, so it'll stop being an edge and become the ordinary thing. I'd need to be better at the human bits: talking to clients, understanding what they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no job turns up in Harbourtown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move. I'd look at the bigger city two hours away, where agencies are, and rent a room with someone for a few months. I'd cut the flat costs, since I'd be paying for a room I don't use. It's a gamble, but a calculated one, and I'm not attached to Harbourtown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, and people should get hands-on with it now. I'd post short how-tos, because it's good for my profile. I'd also say firms ought to train juniors in the tools instead of cutting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think writing posts, planning content and answering customer messages are what I do for the gym, and the software does them faster. So I'm competing with myself, with a cheaper version. My edge is that I know the tools and can talk to owners, but that's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after businesses that can't afford an agency but want results: cafes, trades, and clinics. I'd offer a package, a monthly plan with reports, so I'm not just selling posts. And I'd learn one more tool each month, like video editing or analytics, so I don't stall. I'd also cold-email five agencies a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. I like that the ground is moving, because it gives people like me a way in. But I know I could be replaced just as quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the thinking tasks on the card are the ones you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing captions and ad copy, scheduling posts, replying to comments and making simple reports. About three-quarters of my week at the gym is that. The software does a first draft, and I check and fix it. That's the part where I'm useful today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the gym owner if she asked you whether to fire her social media person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to keep a person who can use the tools, check the output and talk to members. Not a big team, just one good person. It would be a bit awkward if she meant me, but I'd say it anyway.

steps.text: Sell cafes and clinics a monthly marketing package with reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about support now. People will need income help and faster retraining. I'd also say don't panic-buy courses, because most of them will be out of date by the end. I'd keep it short on social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious. If thinking work is mostly done by AI in two years, a marketing junior role isn't there. My advantage is that I'm used to the tools, but so will everyone be. I'd feel the clock more than most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every pound, and keep the gym client and any other local ones as steady cash. I'd move to the bigger city fast, to share a cheap room and be where people hire. I'd also look at hands-on work in the meantime, like events and hospitality, since robots take three more years. And I'd ask Ironside whether I could do some front-desk shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty on edge, but I'd keep moving. I find action easier than worry. At night I'd probably still look at the ceiling, doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spend the two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the sums, eat the cheap stuff, and keep the lease flexible. I'd say it straight: I might leave if I find work elsewhere. They'd probably say go, and one of them would offer to keep my stuff in his room. They're good guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them as a rough income, not a career. A hundred and ten a month won't pay rent, but a few more clients could cover groceries. And the work shows I can deliver. If the thinking jobs go anyway, then at least I'd know people who trust me.

I'd tell people not to panic-buy courses that will be out of date.

Pick up event and hospitality shifts for steady cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway, and young people should use it. I'd tell my friends to build a few real skills and not depend on one job. I'd back training programmes, but I'd be wary of waiting for someone else to organise them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have a fair shot. If I get a first job within a year, I'd get four years of experience to use, and I'd know how to work with the tools. I'd just have to pick a field where people stay in the loop, like client advice and strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still move to the bigger city, but not in a panic. I'd take an agency job, even at a low salary, to learn the ropes. I'd save a hundred pounds a month and pay down some of the loan. And I'd keep two or three clients on the side, so I'm not dependent on one pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite steady, honestly. A bit tense about money, but five years lets me think. It's the first one where I'd feel I can improve my situation instead of just defend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still move to the bigger city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but with more care. Two years means I leave now and take whatever is there. With five I'd choose an agency that trains people and lets me touch real client work. I'd move once I have an offer, which is cheaper than moving and hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you aim to be good at by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Understanding what a business owner really wants and turning it into a plan that works. Machines write the copy; I want to be the one who knows whether it's the right copy. That means talking to customers, reading data and being the person clients phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the one where we can all get ready, so let's get ready. I'd tell people to try the tools now, and I'd tell firms to hire juniors who can learn. I'd feel pretty relaxed saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about my chances. By thirty-three I could have a proper career, maybe running a small agency or leading marketing for a firm, with AI doing the grunt work. I'd still have to get the first job, which is the hard bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job in a small agency or a company marketing team, and keep learning. After a year or two I'd start a side business, maybe helping local firms with AI-based marketing. I'd save two hundred a month once I'm earning, pay the loan down and maybe get a small flat with a friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, really. I'd feel like I can breathe. I'd still have the odd bad week, because the loan doesn't vanish, but I'd see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a whole decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get complacent. Ten years is long, and it's easy to relax and let the tools pass me by. I'd put a reminder in my calendar to learn something new every quarter, and I'd stay close to people who are better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you even then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own flat, a small business and a bit of money for my mum, who's done everything for me. Maybe a trip somewhere warm. Nothing too crazy, but it all depends on that first job.

I still have to get the first job, which is the hard bit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because there's no time to build a track record and I have almost no savings. What would help is a bridge, something like paid placements or income support while I find my feet. And honest advice about what skills last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being good with the tools doesn't mean being safe. People assume young people who use AI will be fine, but I'm in the same boat as everyone else, with a loan and no job yet.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools doesn't mean being safe.
portrait: Ivan (23) shares a flat in **Harbourtown**, owes a big student loan and has about ten days of savings.
He holds a pass in marketing with no internship, and earns a hundred and ten pounds a month from a gym client.
He uses **AI every day**, cold-emails agencies and is willing to move cities.
He is upbeat and practical, choosing **action over worry** in every scenario.
His mood stays anxious until there is a decade, because money is thin and no first job has arrived.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because there'd be no time to build a track record.
whatWouldHelp: A **bridge** such as paid placements or income support, and honest advice about which skills last.
